title: Margin of Error and Sample Size Estimation

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The margin of error (d) is the “±” part of a CI: critical value × standard error. Sample size estimation reverses the CI calculation: fix the margin you can accept, the confidence level and a guess at the variability, and solve for n. For a proportion, n = Z²p(1 − p)/d². For a mean, n = Z²σ²/d².

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Before a survey you decide how precise the answer must be, for example “membership prevalence within ±5 percentage points”. The CI formula links that precision to n, so you can solve for n. The simple formula assumes a simple random sample with everyone responding. Real surveys are clustered and some households do not respond, so the basic n is then inflated in steps (Arya et al., 2012).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Proportion, absolute precision. The margin is d = Z√[p(1 − p)/n]. Square both sides: d² = Z²p(1 − p)/n. Solve for n:

n = Z² p(1 − p)/d²

With Z = 1.96 rounded to 2, Z² = 4, and with q = 1 − p and L the allowable error, this becomes the shortcut n = 4pq/L².

Why p = 0.5 is the safe guess. p(1 − p) = p − p² = 0.25 − (p − 0.5)². The squared term is never negative, so p(1 − p) is at most 0.25, reached at p = 0.5. With no prior estimate, p = 0.5 gives the largest, safest n.

Relative precision. If the margin is set as a fraction ε of p (for example ±20% of p), then d = εp and n = Z²p(1 − p)/(εp)² = Z²q/(ε²p). Rare conditions need relative precision: ±5 points around a prevalence of 3% would be useless.

Mean. d = Zσ/√n gives n = Z²σ²/d², with σ from a pilot study or earlier work.

Halving the margin. n ∝ 1/d², so halving d multiplies n by four.

Finite population correction (FPC). Sampling without replacement from a small population of size N reduces the variance of the estimate by the factor (N − n)/(N − 1) ≈ 1 − n/N (recall the finite population correction checked in §6.5). Setting the reduced variance equal to that of the uncorrected n₀ gives 1/n − 1/N = 1/n₀, so n = n₀/(1 + n₀/N). It matters only when n₀ is more than a few per cent of N.

Design effect. A cluster sample of n gives the precision of a simple random sample of n/DEFF (recall §6.2.6, where DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ was previewed, m being the households per cluster and ρ the intra-cluster correlation). To keep the precision, multiply n by DEFF.

Non-response. If only a fraction r of those approached respond, approach n/r.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Planning a repeat CBHI survey in the district: expected membership p = 0.30, margin ±5 percentage points, 95% confidence, village clusters of 25 households with DEFF 2.44 (m = 25, ρ = 0.06), and 90% expected response.

  1. Simple random sample: n₀ = 1.96² × 0.30 × 0.70/0.05² = 3.8416 × 0.21/0.0025 = 322.7 → 323 households.
  2. Shortcut: 4pq/L² = 4 × 0.21/0.0025 = 336. The small excess comes from rounding 1.96 up to 2.
  3. Without a prior estimate (p = 0.5): 1.96² × 0.25/0.0025 = 384.2 → 385 (or 400 by the shortcut).
  4. Design effect: 322.7 × 2.44 = 787.4.
  5. Non-response: 787.4/0.90 = 874.9 → 875 households, that is, 35 villages of 25.
  6. Relative precision instead: ±20% of 30% means d = 0.06, and n₀ = 3.8416 × 0.70/(0.04 × 0.30) = 224.1 → 225 before the design effect.
  7. FPC, only if the frame were small: if the survey covered a block of just N = 2,500 households, n₀ would fall to 322.7/(1 + 322.7/2,500) = 285.8 → 286 before the design effect.

Check against the survey actually done. The CBHI survey interviewed 500 households in 20 villages. Its effective sample size is 500/2.44 = 205, so its margin is 1.96 × √(0.21/205) = ±6.3 points, not the ±4.0 points a simple random sample of 500 would give. That matches the clustered SE of 0.032 (recall §6.2.6; 1.96 × 0.032 = 0.063). This is why step 5 needs 875 households, not 323, for ±5 points.

A mean. To estimate the mean weight of clinic children within ±0.5 kg, taking σ = 1.75 kg from today’s 30: n = 1.96² × 1.75²/0.5² = 3.8416 × 3.0625/0.25 = 47.1 → 48 children. For ±0.25 kg, n = 188.2 → 189, four times as many.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
z <- qnorm(0.975); p <- 0.30; d <- 0.05
n0 <- z^2 * p * (1 - p) / d^2          # simple random sample
n1 <- n0 * 2.44                          # x design effect
n2 <- n1 / 0.90                          # / expected response
round(c(n0 = n0, with_deff = n1, with_nonresponse = n2), 1)
ceiling(n2 / 25)                         # villages of 25 households
              n0        with_deff with_nonresponse 
           322.7            787.3            874.8 
[1] 35

The three numbers are steps 1, 4 and 5. They differ from the hand values in the first decimal only because R uses z = 1.959964 rather than 1.96. Always round the final n up: 874.8 households means 875, and 35 villages.

points.html: Choosing d. There is no universal rule. One convention is ±5 points when the expected prevalence lies between 10% and 90%, and a margin of about one-quarter to one-fifth of p when p is small (Pourhoseingholi et al., 2013). State and justify your choice.
Order of adjustments. n₀ → FPC (if the frame is small) → × DEFF → ÷ response rate → round up to whole clusters.
What the inflations do not do. Dividing by the response rate keeps the number of respondents up. It does not remove non-response bias if non-responders differ from responders (recall §6.4).

Precision, not power. These formulas give a sample big enough to estimate one quantity precisely. Samples for comparing groups need power calculations (power: the chance that a study detects a difference that really exists; §15.6, where n depends on the smallest difference worth detecting).
A planning guess, not a fact. The n is only as good as the guesses of p, σ and DEFF. When a guess is uncertain, compute n for a range of values and use the largest affordable.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 7.4

questions.prompt: You want to halve the margin of error of a planned prevalence survey. Roughly how much larger must the sample be, and why?
questions.answer: Four times larger. n = Z²p(1 − p)/d², so n ∝ 1/d². Halving d multiplies n by 2² = 4, because the standard error shrinks only with √n.

questions.prompt: Expected anaemia prevalence among adolescent girls is 10%, with a margin of ±3 percentage points at 95% confidence. Compute n₀. Then adjust for a cluster design with DEFF = 2 and 85% expected response.
For the same 10%, what n₀ is needed for a relative precision of ±20%? Why is it larger than in question 2?
questions.answer: d = 0.20 × 0.10 = 0.02. n₀ = Z²q/(ε²p) = 3.8416 × 0.90/(0.04 × 0.10) = 864.4 → 865. It is larger because ±20% of 10% is ±2 points, a tighter margin than the ±3 points of question 2.
